# Outline your whole novel in one sitting with any AI assistant

> **In short:** By copying a six-step prompt chain into any modern AI assistant, you can turn a single sentence about your novel idea into a full chapter-by-chapter outline in one sitting. The chain works the same way in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or Le Chat.

Have you ever had a novel idea bouncing around in your head but stalled at the blank page? In the next 30 to 60 minutes, you can walk from a single sentence to a complete outline, ready for drafting, using nothing but the chat box of an AI assistant you probably already use for email or homework. This guide is for hobby writers, aspiring novelists, and anyone who's been told "you should really write that book" — no prior outlining experience needed.

## Before you start
- A free or paid account with any modern AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or Le Chat. Sign-up takes about two minutes if you don't have one yet.
- One sentence about your novel idea — the roughest draft is fine. Try to include a protagonist (the lead character) and a hint of conflict.
- A notes app, a Word document, or plain paper to save the outline as you go.
- About 30–60 minutes of focused time, and a willingness to push back when an answer doesn't feel right.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat and share your one-line idea
Open your AI assistant and start a brand-new conversation. Look near the top of the sidebar for a button labeled something like **"New chat"**, **"New conversation"**, or a small **+** icon; if you don't see it, check a menu (often a small icon with three dots or three lines) for a "start new" option. Tapping it gives you a clean chat with no memory of past sessions. Type your one-line idea into the message box at the bottom and send. The assistant will reply with something like "Got it — tell me more" or restate your idea in its own words. Don't worry about polish; the messier the input, the more useful the next step becomes.

💬 Example: *A shy baker in a small coastal town discovers a stranger's lost notebook containing recipes that magically bake the eater's happiest memory.*

You'll know it worked when the AI responds by acknowledging your premise in plain English, ready for the next instruction.

## Step 2 — Ask for the three-act skeleton
In the same chat, send a follow-up prompt that asks for the classic three-act structure — meaning the setup, the confrontation, and the resolution, the three big chunks almost every novel uses. The assistant will return something labeled **Act 1**, **Act 2**, and **Act 3**, each with a short paragraph. Read it as a working draft, not a final word. If a section feels off, reply with "make Act 2 darker" or "swap the climax for a quieter ending" — the AI will redraft without losing the rest of the conversation. If your assistant doesn't recognize the term "three-act structure," try "give me a beginning, middle, and end" instead.

💬 Example: *Give me a three-act structure for this story. Keep each act to two or three sentences. Label them Act 1, Act 2, Act 3.*

You'll know it worked when you see three clearly labeled acts, each with its own short paragraph and a distinct purpose.

## Step 3 — Build out your main characters
Now ask the AI to sketch out three to five main characters, including your protagonist (the lead character who drives the story), the antagonist (the force opposing them), and one or two supporting figures who raise the stakes. For each, the assistant should give a name, a one-line goal, a flaw, and why they matter to the plot. If the response feels thin, say "give each character a secret" or "add a best friend who disagrees with the protagonist." The aim here is depth, not perfection; you can rename, merge, or delete anything later.

💬 Example: *Create four main characters for this story. For each, give a name, a goal, a flaw, and one secret. Make sure the protagonist and antagonist can't both win.*

You'll know it worked when each character has all four pieces, and the names feel like they could clash on the page.

## Step 4 — Map the major plot beats of the middle
Ask the AI to break Act 2 into five to seven plot beats — the turning points that move the story forward, moments like "the mentor dies," "the hero refuses the call," or "the midpoint reversal." This is the part of the outline most beginners skip, and it's usually why drafts sag in the middle. The assistant will return a numbered list, each beat tied to a change in the story. Push back if a beat feels weak: "Make beat 3 a betrayal" or "Slow beat 5 down with a quiet scene." If your assistant returns too many or too few beats, ask for exactly the number you want.

💬 Example: *List seven plot beats for Act 2, numbered. After each beat, write one sentence describing what changes because of it. Spread the seven beats across roughly the middle two-thirds of the story.*

You'll know it worked when you have a numbered list, each beat tied to a clear change in the story, and the middle of your novel feels structured instead of vague.

## Step 5 — Turn the beats into a chapter list
Now ask the AI to expand the full outline — Acts 1, 2, and 3, plus the beats — into a chapter list, usually fifteen to twenty-five chapters depending on the genre. Romance and thriller novels tend to be shorter; epic fantasy and family sagas run longer. The assistant will return numbered chapters, each with a working title and a one-line summary. If you want a longer or shorter book, say so: "make it 12 chapters" or "stretch it to 30." Copy the list into your notes app before continuing — that's your working map.

💬 Example: *Turn this outline into 20 chapters. Number them. Give each a short working title and one sentence about what happens.*

You'll know it worked when you can scroll through and see the story move from beginning to end, chapter by chapter, without any obvious gaps.

## Step 6 — Expand each chapter into a paragraph
For your final step, ask the AI to expand the chapter list into paragraph-long summaries — what the reader learns, what changes, and which characters appear. Send the request in one go if your outline is short, or in two or three chunks if it's long; an AI assistant can handle large prompts, but a chat with a very long output may cut off mid-paragraph. Read every chapter summary once and flag any that feel rushed or off-tone; a quick "redo chapter 12 with more dialogue" usually fixes it. Be aware that the AI can draft an outline, but it can't write the novel for you — that part still needs your voice, your hours, and your judgment.

💬 Example: *Take the 20 chapters above and expand each into a paragraph (4–6 sentences). Include the main character's emotional state at the end of the chapter.*

You'll know it worked when you have a complete chapter-by-chapter outline you could hand to a friend, and they could follow the whole story without you explaining it.

## Common mistakes
- **Starting a new chat halfway through.** Each new conversation loses everything you've built so far. Stay in the same chat for all six steps; the assistant keeps the context (the running history of the conversation) live.
- **Accepting the first answer.** AI drafts are first drafts. If a chapter summary feels flat, ask for a redraft — "darker," "more romantic," "more suspenseful." Pushback is part of the process, not a sign of failure.
- **Skipping Step 4.** New writers often jump from a vague idea to a chapter list and wonder why the middle drags. The plot-beat step is what gives a novel its shape; treat it as the spine, not a luxury.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Outline your next hobby project — a short story, a memoir, even a non-fiction book — using the same six steps, and you'll start writing with a map instead of a blank page.
- **For your business or work:** The same chain works for a course curriculum, a podcast season, or a multi-part blog series; "chapters" become episodes or modules.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't polish your one-line idea before sending it. The point of the AI is to help you find the shape of the story, not to reward a finished pitch.

## Try it now
Open any AI assistant you already have an account with, paste your one-line idea into a new chat, and copy in the Step 1 example prompt. You've started your outline.
